newsitem.title: INDIA: India wants talks with Pakistan, but waits for nod.
newsitem.headline: India wants talks with Pakistan, but waits for nod.

text.p: India said on Wednesday it favoured resuming high-level talks with Pakistan but would wait for prime minister-elect Nawaz Sharif to take the first step in bridging differences between the long-time foes.
"We will fully cooperate with Islamabad," the Press Trust of India (PTI) quoted Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda as telling reporters during an official visit to Mauritius.
"Let him (Sharif) first assume office and extend an official invitation to us for talks," Deve Gowda was quoted as saying.

Deve Gowda was quoted by United News of India (UNI) as saying Sharif, whose Pakistan Muslim League won a resounding majority in general elections held on Monday, had expressed a desire to hold talks at foreign minister level.
Talks involving foreign secretaries -- the highest civil servants in the two nations' foreign ministries -- broke down in early 1994.

"Once we get an invitation after Mr Sharif takes charge, we will fully cooperate with Pakistan in the first stage of talks at foreign ministers' level," UNI quoted the Indian prime minister as saying.

Defence Minister Mulayam Singh Yadav was quoted by UNI as saying Deve Gowda had written letters to ousted Pakistani prime minister Benazir Bhutto, whose Pakistan People's Party was humiliated in the polls, but received no satisfactory reply.
"If the new government in Pakistan wants cordial relations with India, we welcome it," UNI quoted Singh as saying.

India and Pakistan have fought three wars since they were carved out of British India in a bloody partition in 1947. Two of the conflicts have been sparked by tension in the Himalayan region of Kashmir, which is divided between the two nations.

The chief minister of India's Jammu and Kashmir state, Farooq Abdullah, was quoted earlier on Wednesday as saying India and Pakistan should agree that the line of control dividing Kashmir should become a permanent border.
His comments sparked heated criticism from senior leaders of the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) as well as the Congress party.

"Any such concession will amount to violating India's territorial integrity," UNI quoted BJP general secretary K.N. Govindacharya as saying. "Dr Farooq Abdullah cannot be unaware of these implications of his outrageous suggestion."
